candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: A secular preference-based account makes the moral status of an action vary with recipients' preferences and therefore cannot supply an objective standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and Slick's explicit second-person criticism clearly attribute this sustained objection to Matt Slick.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly attacks Clifton's proposed secular foundation by arguing that its dependence on preferences produces incompatible moral verdicts for the same action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's contractualist and harm-oriented explanation of why an unobserved rape remains morally wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: After Clifton introduces a veil-of-ignorance contractual model, Slick argues that preference-sensitive judgments make identical conduct good or bad depending on the recipient.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: A divine moral theory is circular because God can be evaluated as the moral standard only by appealing back to God himself.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly contrasts his nuanced moral system with Slick's system and states the circularity objection in his own turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges the explanatory adequacy of the proposed divine foundation and tests it with the possibility of a God who desires universal misery.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's demand for a concise secular moral standard and his claim that God's revealed character supplies one.

candidates.contextSummary: Responding to Slick's request for a compact standard, Clifton says moral inquiry is necessarily more complex and argues that defining God through God is circular.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Secular moral definitions are arbitrary because they rest in personal choice, whereas moral truth rests in God's revealed character rather than human intuition.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick expressly contrasts morality grounded in God's character with morality grounded in Clifton's character and cites divine revelation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states Slick's principal grounding distinction between divine revelation and human preference, directly supporting the pro side's answer to the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that moral intuitions can be evaluated against the meanings assigned to right and wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of intuition and arbitrariness, Slick maintains that revealed prohibitions allow moral knowledge without recursively validating one's own intuitions.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Divine-command morality can in principle separate right and wrong entirely from suffering, happiness, health, and other real-world consequences.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces the objection as a problem with Slick's worldview and develops the universal-misery hypothetical directly.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument contests whether God's nature supplies a substantively credible moral foundation by showing that it could label maximal misery moral by definition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's assertion that conduct such as homosexual relationships is wrong whenever God declares it wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: After Slick treats divine declaration as decisive, Clifton argues that this account can disregard welfare entirely and again invokes a universal-misery counterexample.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Atheism cannot justify a non-subjective objective moral standard, while Christian obligation follows from God's nature, human creation for his glory, and eventual judgment.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick resumes his lost train of thought, addresses Clifton by name, and delivers an extended first-person defense of the Christian position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a direct affirmative case for the motion, combining a transcendental objection to secular morality with a practical illustration of allegedly unanswerable moral wrongdoing.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's request for a reason to adopt Slick's worldview and his statement that threatened consequences may not motivate him.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick argues that secular appeals to harm or social agreement are unjustified preferences and illustrates the claimed result with a coercive theft scenario.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Even complete acceptance of Christianity's factual and moral claims does not by itself provide a motivating reason that compels someone to obey them.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly sets up and repeatedly clarifies a role-playing counterexample in which he accepts every proposition in Slick's worldview.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The thought experiment targets the gap between identifying an act as divinely prohibited and supplying an action-guiding reason, exposing a central normative challenge to theism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's claim that accepting his Christian worldview would prevent a person from committing grave wrongdoing.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton imagines accepting Christianity while intending to molest a baby, then argues that beliefs about God, punishment, and wrongness remain descriptions or prescriptions he can disregard.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Christians may knowingly violate moral requirements, but inconsistency between belief and practice does not undermine the existence of objective moral truth.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick introduces the revised scenario, cites his counseling experience, and explicitly distinguishes Christian profession from inconsistent practice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This answers Clifton's motivational counterexample by separating moral ontology from compliance and restates the charge that atheism lacks an objective standard.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's scenario in which someone accepts every Christian proposition yet still intends to commit an atrocity.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick concedes that believers can act against acknowledged duties, treats this as inconsistency rather than disproof, and renews his challenge to atheistic condemnation.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: An action can possess inherent moral rightness or wrongness only if an absolute God identifies it as consistent or inconsistent with his nature.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick explicitly frames the issue as moral ontology and contrasts an absolute divine nature with an atheistic worldview.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The proposition gives the pro side's direct metaphysical answer to the debate by claiming that intrinsic moral properties require an absolute divine foundation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that consequences, rather than God, are the relevant standard for evaluating morality.

candidates.contextSummary: During clarification about consequences, Slick distinguishes consequences after an act from the act's moral essence and argues atheistic definitions remain intuitive and arbitrary.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Moral status is not intrinsic to actions but arises from their real-world consequences together with agents' intentions and related circumstances.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly identifies this as a major difference between their views and states his own account in direct contrast to Slick's.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the con side's affirmative alternative to intrinsic divine morality by locating moral evaluation in consequences, intentions, and contextual features.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's contention that actions have an ontological moral essence grounded only in an absolute God's nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton crystallizes the disagreement by denying inherent moral status and offering a consequence-and-intention account as the secular basis for evaluating conduct.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Defining right as what ought to be done does not establish that God's commands are right, because no reason has been supplied for the claimed obligation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton conditionally accepts Slick's definition of right and then directly disputes the unsupported identification of divine commands with obligation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This exposes a purported inferential gap between divine commands and normative authority, challenging whether the proposed foundation actually yields duties for agents.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's assertion that one ought to follow what is right simply because right means what ought to be followed.

candidates.contextSummary: At the core boundary, Clifton accepts the definitional link between rightness and obligation but denies that Slick has connected God's commands to that category.
